Michigan DEQ Coastal Management Program – Program Enhancement Project

## **Bird and Bat Use of Islands and Coastal Areas of Northern Lake Michigan Final Report**

Nancy E. Seefelt Assistant Professor - Biology Central Michigan University Mt. Pleasant, MI 48859 seefe1ne@cmich.edu

## **Abstract**

In 2012, a project using remote acoustic monitoring, as well as traditional avian censusing methods, was undertaken to ascertain bird use of coastal areas in northern Lake Michigan, including islands of the Beaver Archipelago (Charlevoix Co.) and mainland locations in both the Lower Peninsula (Leelanau Co. and Emmet Co.) and Upper Peninsula (Mackinac Co.). Additionally, acoustics were used to determine bat use of these same habitats. Data indicates that there is substantial bird and bat movement through northern Lake Michigan coastal areas and islands during both spring and fall migration.  Many species appear ubiquitous across the region, while others were detected at only one or two locations. Traditional methods of avian censusing (including the area search method and point counts), mistnetting and acoustic monitoring show both similarities and differences in determining the presence of specific species; more work is needed to better understand strengths and disadvantages of acoustic monitoring. Acoustic monitoring data show that, depending on the season, weather variables, as well as the date, may prove useful in predicting bird and bat movements through the region. Acoustic monitoring data was also useful in developing regional maps to visualize the spatial distribution of birds and bats relative to monitoring locations temporally.  Acoustic monitoring is a useful tool for providing a better understanding of migration patterns, including abundance and timing, for birds and bats.  Data should prove valuable as resource managers evaluate the possibility of development of islands and coastal areas of northern Lake Michigan for wind power.

## **Introduction**

The monitoring of bird populations during their annual cycle has been a long-established need in avian conservation.  In addition, bat migration corridors are not well known. Many monitoring centers have been established in the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes Region (primarily for birds) and the information gathered is invaluable for conservation.  However, there are many areas within the region where there is little information on bird and bat use and movement.  As traditional methods in avian monitoring on a regional scale and radar can be cost prohibitive, the expansion of newer technologies is important, especially in remote locations.  Acoustic monitoring has the potential to allow for more comprehensive monitoring coverage at relatively low cost. This project was aimed at establishing acoustic monitoring for both birds and bats as a valuable tool in northern Lake Michigan.  Data can provide a better understanding of migration corridors and stopover habitats with respect to meteorological conditions and changing weather patterns, as well as aid in decisions regarding the development of wind resources.

Beginning in spring (April) 2012 through fall (October) 2012, acoustic monitoring devices designed specifically for bird detection and for bat detection were deployed in coastal areas of Lake Michigan. These devices were programmed to remotely monitor migration and breeding season use by recording the vocalizations of both birds and bats (details below); this report is specific to migration data.  Avian acoustic monitors were outfitted with both standard microphones (diurnal bird vocalizations) and night

flight call microphones (to capture vocalizations during migrant passage at night).  In addition to passerines, night flight call studies can monitor woodpecker, heron, waterfowl and rail nocturnal movements (Farnsworth 2005, Farnsworth & Russell 2005). Separate ultrasonic sensitive devices were used to collect bat vocalizations.  Essentially, acoustic devices have more continuous coverage compared to more time intensive methodologies, such as point counts that can record only snapshots of activity.   Remote acoustic monitoring has been used successfully in other systems to quantify birds (Evans & Mellinger 1999, Evans & Rosenberg 2000, Evans _et al_ . 2007, Blumstein _et al_ . 2011) and bats (Gannon & Bogdanowicz 2000, Weller _et al_ . 2007).   Acoustic monitoring is relatively inexpensive and extremely reliable in discerning birds (including individual species and species groups), as well as different bat species; the equipment has been field tested and data collection is not impeded by adverse weather conditions, such as mist, fog and light rain.  More expensive methods, including thermal imaging and radar technologies, cannot discern species, cannot record birds and bat activities close to the ground, and are sensitive to weather conditions and topographical features (Evans et al 2007). Aerial surveys are not feasible to sample small landbirds and are not effective at night.  The ability to monitor during adverse weather conditions, as well as at night, using acoustic monitoring provides insight regarding the impacts weather has on migration. By combining both night flight call (nocturnal) monitoring with diurnal monitoring, species that do not make night flight calls can be detected with the devices during the dawn chorus.  The continued censusing and constant effort mist netting program on Beaver Island (Spring 2012) in combination with the remote acoustic monitoring has begun to illuminate some potential bias in this study (see below).

Recently, Michigan’s Governor Snyder signed an agreement with four other Great Lakes state governors and the Obama Administration to form the Great Lakes Off-Shore Wind Energy Consortium “to support efforts to achieve an efficient, expeditious, orderly and responsible review of proposed offshore wind energy projects in the American side of the Great Lakes” (Recharge 2012).  Ten years ago, an estimated 33,000 birds were killed through collisions with turbines (USFWS 2002) and with the increasing demand for wind power development in Michigan (Stemler 2007) this number is likely to rise.  Therefore, more research is necessary to better understand migration corridors, especially for species of concern, to aid in the design of a regional framework for wind development. The northern Lake Michigan region is considered to have highly desirable wind resources (USDE 2004), but has also been shown to be a major migration corridor, especially during spring (Diehl et al. 2003, Gehring et al. 2010)

The objectives of this study were to:

1. Use remote acoustic monitoring surveys to identify and quantify bird and bat use patterns in coastal habitats of the Beaver Archipelago (Charlevoix County) and on surrounding mainland locations in the Lower Peninsula (Leelanau and Emmet Counties) and the Upper Peninsula (Mackinac County) during 2012 to aid in the siting of future wind power development.

2. Continue spring (2012) stopover migration census and mist-netting program on Beaver Island for direct comparison with acoustic monitoring data to better evaluate bird detectability by each method.

3. Investigate how adverse weather conditions impact avian migration using acoustic monitoring data.

4. Digitize all acoustic data and provide spatially explicit data to map use patterns in the study areas to better illustrate the importance of coastal habitats to these species

## **Methods**

## Study Area

The Beaver Archipelago (Charlevoix County), as well as coastal areas in the Lower Peninsula (Leelanau and Emmet Counties) and the Upper Peninsula (Mackinac County) were the study area for this project (Table 1, Figure 1). Beaver is the largest of an extensive archipelago; this island group currently represents relatively undeveloped, protected lands (including local conservation organization holdings, state lands and National Wildlife Refuge lands) and appears to provide important migration corridors in the region (Diehl et al. 2003, Gehring et al. 2010, current study).  Beaver Island, although relatively undeveloped compared to some mainland locations, has private land development along the shoreline (primarily summer homes) while the other archipelago islands are not developed.  Both High and Hog Islands are publicly owned state lands. The coastal zone areas on the mainland represent potential important migration corridors and are state-owned properties, including Leelanau State Park (Leelanau County), Wilderness State Park (Emmet County) and Lake Superior State Forest (Mackinac County). Little information is available regarding landbird migration at these locations, however, studies in the Les Cheneaux islands area of northern Lake Huron (Chippewa and Mackinac Counties) indicate that coastal habitats are important to migrants, especially during spring (Ewert & Hamas 1995, Seefelt 1997, Smith _et al_ . 1998, Smith _et al_ . 2004).  Although some presence-absence data are available for bats, little information regarding the current status of bat migration is available for any of these sites.

This project was divided into three components: 1) acoustic monitoring, 2) traditional avian methods, and 3) data entry and analysis.

_1. Acoustic Monitoring_ : A total of fourteen acoustic monitors (Song Meter SM2+, Wildlife Acoustics) were deployed in April or early May (High and Hog Islands) to document bird use of northern Lake Michigan islands and coastal habitats (Table 1, Figure 1).  Additionally, six bat acoustic monitors (SM2BAT, Wildlife Acoustics) were deployed on each island and at each mainland location (Table 1, Figure 1). Both bird and bat monitors were placed at the edge of forest habitats on the shoreline.  Each avian monitor  included a standard microphone (SMX-II, Wildlife Acoustic) to record diurnal calls and a specialized microphone (SMX-Night Flight) to record night flight (nocturnal) vocalizations. The avian monitors were programmed to record the dawn chorus beginning roughly 15 minutes before dawn and continuing for an hour.  In addition, they recorded 15 minutes out of every dark hour beginning at sunset and ending when diurnal recordings began. The six bat acoustic monitors with ultrasonic microphones (SMX-US, Wildlife Acoustics) were programmed to record 15 minutes out of every dark hour from dusk to dawn.  These methodologies allowed for adequate sampling while simultaneously allowing for efficiency in data storage and battery life. Each monitor was programmable to its specific location (GPS coordinates) so that it tracked changes in sunset and sunrise times. Monitors were checked in June and August, and retrieved in September (High and Hog Islands due to changing/dangerous lake conditions in the fall) or October (other sites).

_2. Traditional Avian Methods:_ The standard methodologies that were conducted during spring migration at the CMU Biological Station on Beaver Island included constant-effort mist-netting (and banding) and censusing using the area search method and point counts (Ralph _et al_ . 1993, Hussel & Ralph 1998). One of the acoustic monitors (Sand Bay) is located at this site. Mist-nets at eighteen permanent sites were unfurled within 30 minutes of local sunrise throughout the spring migration period, and remained open for approximately 6 hours each day, weather permitting.  Nets were not operated during inclement conditions to ensure the safety of the birds.  Each net will was checked within every 20 minutes. Captured birds were be removed from the nets and placed in cotton holding bags labeled with net number/location.  Birds were then transported to the central processing location for data collection and banding. Weather conditions, including temperature, wind speed, and humidity, were collected at the Beaver Island study site on each research day when nets were opened and closed.   The mist-netting component allowed for a better estimation on the condition of migrants (related study), and also allowed for the detection of species that tend to be more silent during migration and could prove difficult to detect using auditory cues and acoustics.

The area search method was used to census all birds at the study site every other day.  Birds were identified by both sight and ear, and recorded by speaking into an audio recorder that was later transcribed.  The census will followed a pre-determined 400 m route that was established in 2006, and each census was completed within one hour of sunrise. Methodology follows protocols that have been used by important bird monitoring stations (Gulf Coast, Rocky Point, Whitefish Point and Long Point Bird Observatories).  On alternate days, five minute point counts were completed at four permanent locations imbedded in the census route and mist-net array following standard protocols; point counts were also be completed within one hour of sunrise (Ralph _et al_ . 1993).  Censuses were not performed on days of high winds and rain.

_3. Data Entry & Analysis:_ Data were entered into data bases as collected.  Avian acoustic data was processed using _Song Scope_ (Wildlife Acoustics) and _RavenPro_ (Cornell Lab of Ornithology); an existing guide (Evans & O’Brien 2002), as well as other published recorded bird song (i.e. Peterson Guide to Eastern Bird Songs), were used to aid in vocalization identification. Bat acoustic data was processed using _Sonobat_ (Sonobat Software); this program provides reference bat calls for comparison. Both avian and bat data were compiled to investigate similarities and differences in site use of  species groups (birds) and specific species (birds and bats) during both spring and fall migration.

After compilation, avian night flight (nocturnal) spring and fall data were compared using t-tests to determine any differences in the number individual birds detected and the number of species detected each night.  Additionally, spring and fall night flight data were compared using t-tests by species group, List A (neotropical migrants), List B (nearctic migrants) and other species, to examine difference in the numbers of birds and species detected each night. (Avian lists are published in Faaborg, 2002.) Bat acoustic data collected in spring and fall were also compared using t-tests to determine if there were differences between the average number of bats detected per night and the number of species of bat detected per night.  For both birds and bats, data from all sites were combined for these comparisons.

Data collected at the CMUB Biological Station (Sand Bay site) on Beaver Island using the traditional methods of avian census and point counts were compiled.  The number of avian species detected by each method was compared using a Mann Whitney Test.  As data were similar, these were combined and compared separately to diurnal and night-flight acoustic data using Mann Whitney Tests.  The number of avian species detected each day by diurnal and each night by nocturnal monitoring was compared using a Mann Whitney Test.  Additionally, data collect by the traditional methods, acoustic

methods and mist-netting were examined to determine any differences in species specific detection at the study site.

Generalized linear models were developed to examine which weather variables could predict migration intensity for birds and for bats. Weather variables were obtained from the Beaver Island airport (KSJX; 45.6925, -85.5636) due to its centralized location between all monitors. These variables included temperature (Fahrenheit; model variable name: Temp), dew point (F; DewPt), sea level pressure (in. Hg; Pressure) wind speed (miles per hour, WindMPH), wind direction (degrees, WindDir), the wind gust speed (miles per hour, GustMPH), visibility (miles; Vis), Humidity (Hum), and weather events (e.g. Fog, rain, drizzle, etc).  All numerical variables were averaged over 24 hours. The estimated percentage of the day that was overcast (Overcast), light rain or drizzle were observed (LightRaindrizzle), moderate to heavy rain was observed (Rain), or fog/haze was present (Fog), was calculated from the weather events by combining events into categories and dividing the counts of each category by the total count of events for the past 24 hours. A categorical variable for the presence of high-speed gusts during the 24 hours (0=no gusts, 1=gusts present) was derived from the average gust wind speed (GustYes). The day of the year was also included as a variable (DayofYear). The number of birds (List A,  List B, Other, and Total) observed during night flights in the spring (21 April 2012 - 31 May 2012) and fall (15 August 2012 – 30 September 2012) was averaged across all monitors to account for missing monitor information from certain days due to poor weather or other monitor problems. This procedure was replicated for bat detections.

A full model that contained every weather variable and DayofYear was constructed for each one of the independent variables (mean number of spring night flight birds observed by species groups: TotalADetect, TotalBDetect, OtherDetect, TotalDetect; mean number of fall  night flight birds observed by species groups: TotalADetect, TotalBDetect, OtherDetect, TotalDetect;  the number of unique species observed each spring day for night flight and dawn chorus birds: NightSpp, DawnSpp; Mean number of bat detections by season: AllMeanDetections, SpringMeanDetections, FallMeanDetections). All iterations of variables within each full model were generated and ranked by AICc using the R package glmulti (Calcagno and de Mazancourt 2010).

Visual interpretation of repeated count data across a landscape is difficult without an approximation of scale and intensity.  ArcMap 10’s Inverse distance weighting (IDW) was used to create interpolated maps of bird and bat density across the study region. Due to the low number of monitor stations spread across a large geographic area, using interpolation methods come with some risk in this study; maps produced are for visualization purposes only and can only provide rough estimations of true densities. Indicator kriging, the recommended modeling procedure for bird count interpolation (Walker et al. 2008), was not always possible with the low number of monitor locations.  For reproducibility and ease of understanding, IDW was used in all cases (power = 2).

## **Results**

## Acoustic Data

The date of deployment and retrieval of both bird and bat monitors varied by site (Tables 2 and 3). Monitoring for birds during spring migration began sooner on Beaver Island and mainland sites compared to High and Hog Islands due to accessibility.  A late start on McCauley Point, Beaver Island and an early end date at the Hog Island - Northeast location during spring migration were due to malfunctions of those devices. During fall migration, some devices ended recording early due to short battery life, with the exception of the High Island North site, where a microphone cable broke due to high winds.   Monitoring for bats during spring migration began sooner at mainland sites compared to

islands locations due to late equipment arrival (Beaver Island) and inaccessibility (High and Hog Islands). Differences in the length of bat monitor activity were primarily due to battery power demand. For bat monitors, more power is needed by the monitor when bats are present and their calls trigger recording during the 15 minute survey blocks. More energy is used by the monitor when bats are present than when bats are not.

During spring migration, 125 avian species (excluding gulls and waterfowl) were recorded in the study area using both diurnal and nocturnal acoustic monitoring (all sites combined), including 54 List A (neotropical migrant) species, 28 List B (nearctic migrant) species, as well as 46 other species (Table 4). During fall migration, 68 avian species (excluding gulls and waterfowl) were recorded in the study area using only nocturnal acoustic monitoring (all sites combined), including 29 List A species, 17 List B species, as well as 22 other species (Table 5).  Only nocturnal acoustics were used during fall migration

as there was little dawn chorusing; diurnal data will still be investigated to determine if other species not detected at night are present at each location.

Of the 125 species (excluding gulls and waterfowl) detected by diurnal and nocturnal acoustic monitoring during spring migration, 39 species (31%) were detected at all six monitoring locations (Table 6). Multiple monitors at each location were combined for this compilation. Additionally, there were 23 species (18%) that were detected at only one of the six locations (Table 6).   Of the 68 species (excluding gulls and waterfowl) detected by nocturnal acoustic monitoring during fall migration, 17 species (25%) were detected at all six monitoring locations while 13 (19%) were detected at only one.  Multiple monitors at each site were again combined for this compilation.  Some difference in species detection during fall migration reflects the use of nocturnal acoustic recordings only; some species (i.e. AMCR and RBNU) were most likely present at multiple sites but did not vocalize during the dark hours at several locations.

A total of 7,981 bird vocalizations were detected using nocturnal monitoring during spring migration, while there were 8,460 detections during fall migration.  The differences in total numbers most likely reflect that the number of monitor days was greater in the fall.  When the average number of detections per night (all active monitors combined each night) were compared between spring and fall migration, more birds were detected in spring than in fall [t(86)= 2.59, p=0.011] each night (Figure 2).  There were no differences in the number of individual List A birds detected [t(86)=-.1.60, p=0.112] or the number of detections of other birds [t(86)=-0.15, p=0.879] between the spring and fall migration periods. However, the number of List B birds detected each night was higher in the spring than in the fall [t(86)=3.26, p=0.002).  When the average number of bird species detected per night (all active monitors combined each night) were compared between spring and fall migration, more species were detected in spring than in fall [t(86)=7.68, p=0.000] each night (Figure 3).  This trend was true for all groups of the birds, List A [t(86)=2.50,p=0.014], List B [t(86)=7.23, p=0.000] and other species [t(86)=7.42, 0.000].

It was difficult to determine if more than one bat of the same species was calling during a single 15 minute sampling period.  Therefore, only one bat per species was counted during each 15 minute sampling period.  Thus, the number of detections indicates the minimum number of bats present; it is likely that more bats were present at each location on any given night. When the average number of bats detected (as defined above) per night (all active monitors combined) were compared between spring and fall migration, more bats were detected in fall than in spring [t(77)=-2.16, p=0.034] each night (Figure 4).  Similarly, when the average number of bat species detected per night (all active monitors combined) were compared between spring and fall migration, more species were detected in fall than in spring [t(77)=-2.29, p=0.025] each night (Figure 5).

## Comparison of Traditional Methods & Acoustics

The traditional methods of censusing, point counts and mist netting for spring migration began on 07 May 2012, and ended on 01 June 2012, at the CMU Biological Station on Beaver Island.  Because of weather constraints, a total of 11 censuses (area search method), 10 point count days, and 20 mistnetting days were completed in spring 2012. Some mist-netting days were shortened due to changes in weather (wind strengthening, rain beginning, etc.) but on most days, mist nets were open approximately 6 hours. The number of bird species detected by the area search and point count methods were compared; no differences were detected between the two methods [U(19)=141.5, p=0.159].  Because these data were similar, they were combined (hereafter, the traditional methods) and compared to the acoustic data.  Additionally, a total of 186 birds were captured in the mist nets.

The number of bird species detected by the traditional methods was greater than the number detected by diurnal acoustic recording [U(42)=689.5, p=0.000] each day (Figure 6).  Similarly, the number of

species detected each day using traditional methods was greater than the number of species detected by nocturnal acoustic recording [U(42)=609.0, p=0.000] each night (Figure 6).  These differences most like reflect the greater area, as well as multiple habitats, censused by the traditional methods.   Some species may be more likely to occur in specific habitats and mobile flocks are more likely to be encountered over a larger area.  Acoustic recording was conducted at only one location embedded within the larger area covered by traditional censusing.  The number of species detected with acoustic monitoring diurnally and nocturnally were similar to each other [U(46)=583.5, p=0.9343] (Figure 6).

## Impacts of Weather

Top-ranked generalized linear models with significant predictor variables were generated for each group of birds and bats in relation to weather. The top five models for each group are shown in Tables 11-14. The relatively low AICc weights reported are likely due to the large number of variables in the full model and the possibility of interactions. Day of year (date) was the most common variable in the top-ranked models (#1 of 5 models), followed by wind direction and wind speed. During the night flight in the spring, more birds were associated with days earlier in the season (negative association with DayofYear), whereas in the fall more birds were associated with days later in the season (positive association with DayofYear) (Table 15). In general, birds flew at times with higher temperatures, however, List B birds flew at lower temperatures in the spring. In the spring during the night flight, wind speed was only important in one model (List B species) with higher winds having a positive effect, but in the fall higher wind speeds had negative effects on bird densities (all groups and the total group). As would be expected, rain and drizzle had negative effects on bird densities during the night flight (List B and Other species).

For the number of bird species observed during the night flight and the dawn chorus in the spring, both increased with increases in sea level pressure, which could bring clear skies (Table 16). During the night, there were increasing numbers of species with an increase in temperature, and during the day an increase in day of year, which are similar measures (as temperature should also be rising as days go by in the spring). Temperature may be more important at night, because it is likely to be cooler for migrants than those in the dawn chorus, whereas day of year would be more important for the dawn chorus because as bird species migrate to the areas around the monitor they are more likely to stay as time goes by. Interestingly, birds often traveled during times when it was overcast. This may be an artifact of how weather events were modeled: overcast days are probably preferred over rainy or foggy events, and it is probably more likely to be overcast than clear in the spring in general.

## Mapping

A total of 108 maps were produced using the IDW interpolation method (Figures 7-26). Looking at the season (spring and fall) totals for night flight birds, most birds from List A were found in the northern and eastern parts of the study area. Likewise, List B birds were likely to be found in the Upper Peninsula in the fall, but were also dense along the southern part of Beaver Island in the spring and the fall (Figure 7). The highest number of unique species for both the night flight data and the dawn chorus occurred near the southern part of Beaver Island (Figure 8). Interestingly, a higher number of unique species was observed along the Leelanau peninsula during the dawn chorus than during the night.

Large numbers of birds (all groups) were observed during weeks 1-3 in the spring during the night (Figure 9). Is it apparent that birds from List B and other species made up most of the birds in the trend observed in Figure 9 (Figures 10-12). During the first week of the spring monitoring, high numbers of unique species were observed on the southern part of Beaver Island, and increased throughout the region from weeks 2 to 5.  Hot spots differed through time (Figure 13). In the fall, the night flight numbers overall show a large increase in the number of birds during week 4 in the northern and eastern portions of the study area, a decrease during weeks 5 and 6, but then a great increase during week 7 toward the southern part of the region (Figure 14). Birds from List A were concentrated in the north in the fall, and decreased greatly after week 5 (Figure 15). Birds from List B were mostly absent in the region until week 7, when large numbers were observed on the southern part of Beaver Island (Figure 16).  Other species were not detected in sufficient numbers during the fall to provide an accurate visualization of their patterns.

Obviously different trends occur between distributions of birds in the dawn chorus and the night flight. In the dawn chorus, large numbers of birds were observed in the Leelanau Peninsula during weeks 3 and 4 (Figure 17). More birds from List B were observed in week 1 than birds from List A for the dawn chorus. In general, birds from List B were more common earlier in the season, especially in the Leelanau Peninsula, than birds from List A (Figure 18 and 19). Other species were more abundant at the southern end of Beaver Island in week 1, but became more evenly distributed across the area in subsequent weeks; however, hot spots were noted note only on Beaver Island, but also on the Leelanau Peninsula and Waugshance Point especially in week 3 (Figure 20). The number of unique species observed during the dawn chorus, as mentioned previously, was high in the Leelanau Peninsula. This trend began in week 2 and lasted until week 5 when the number of species started to lessen and become more evenly distributed (Figure 21).

For bats, the highest number of species occurred during the fall, shifting from Hog Island in the spring to High Island in the fall (Figure 22). In the spring, the mean number of bat detects was low, but much higher in the fall, especially on Hog and High islands (Figure 23). In the spring, bat detections stayed higher in the northern areas like High Island and in the Upper Peninsula (Figure 24). By the fall, bat numbers were much higher in the north, but then decreased drastically throughout the region by the third week of the fall (Figure 25). The distributions of Big Brown Bats and Little Brown Myotis, the two most numerous bats detected, are distinctly different from one another (Figure 26). Big Brown Bats were detected more on Hog Island and High Island, whereas Little Brown Myotis were detected more often on the mainland in the Upper Peninsula and east of Beaver Island.

## **Conclusions**

Acoustic monitoring for birds and bats during both spring and fall has provided new information regarding migration patterns on islands and coastal areas of northern Lake Michigan.  In general, acoustics successfully documented bird and bat species, as well as provided information on the abundance of birds and bats moving through the region in reference to monitoring locations. It is likely that an increase in monitoring stations would further illuminate migration patterns in the region. Traditional methods of avian censusing (area search and point counts) and mist-netting can provide more detailed information at specific locations, but acoustic monitoring appears to be a viable method for collecting data over a larger geographic area and also during the night when traditional methods are not possible.  As expected, migration timing in the both spring and fall is influenced by date, with some species moving sooner or later than others, depending on the season.  Additional parameters including temperature, wind (direction and magnitude), and other atmospheric conditions (pressure, visibility, precipitation) can all help explain the abundance and movement of migrants on any particular night. More data is needed to best examine these impacts.  The maps produced using acoustic data provide

broad-scale visualizations of bird and bat movements in reference to monitor locations, including indications of avian and bat biodiversity and how this changes temporally.

In essence, data collected through this project provides an initial look at the importance of island and coastal habitats in northern Lake Michigan and emphasizes the need for further investigation prior to development of wind energy resources in this region. According to the Great Lakes Wind Council, “very high concentrations of birds or bats on at least a seasonal basis” are important biocriteria for understanding possible impact development may have on coastal and off-shore resources (Great Lakes Wind Council 2010).  Knowing the species composition of these flocks aids in predicting possible impacts on species of concern.

_Future Steps_ :  We plan to continue to examine existing data to better investigate species specific migration timing and routes; however more data will be needed to better delineate any patterns, especially yearly variations.  We also would like to compare these data with those collected elsewhere in the Great Lakes region, to understand movements on a broader geographic scale.  Acoustic data was also collected during the breeding season and these data still need investigation. We also plan to measure both local habitat parameters and broader level land use patterns to better explain differences in species composition and use at monitoring locations.  Additionally, we plan to further statistically analyze spatial data and continued the use of acoustic monitoring to compare among years, especially in reference to weather patterns.
